    LiteLLM PyPI Package and Docker Images Compromised to Steal Cloud and AI Credentials
    socket.dev · 21 Oct 2026 13:41 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGSberriaidocker-hubgithub-actionsgithub-container-registrylitellmmaturinprivcollectpypipython-startup-hookssitecustomizesocketupwind
    In plain words

    A malicious copy of LiteLLM version 1.107.0, a widely used tool for connecting software to AI services, was published along with related container images. It can run automatically when Python starts and collect passwords, cloud-account access details, private keys, browser data, and AI service login files. Anyone who installed or ran that version, including companies using it in automated builds or online services, may have exposed sensitive access information that could be used to reach their systems or accounts.

    Summary
    LiteLLM version 1.107.0 and related container images were compromised with Python startup-hook malware that steals cloud, AI-tool, browser, and private-key credentials and can fetch unauthenticated remote code. Organizations that installed or ran it should immediately isolate affected environments, rebuild from a trusted version or image digest, and rotate all potentially exposed secrets.

    LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was published with malicious Python startup files in all seven distributed PyPI wheels, and related LiteLLM container images were also reported as affected. The files can run during normal Python startup without an application importing LiteLLM, allowing them to collect cloud credentials, private keys, browser data, AI-tool authentication files, environment variables, and other accessible secrets. Because LiteLLM receives approximately 23 million weekly downloads, affected installations may coexist with provider API keys, cloud identities, database credentials, and deployment secrets.

    The malicious wheel used cook.pth to import cook at Python startup and sitecustomize.py as another startup path, meaning launching Python or pip in an affected environment can activate the payload. The collector encrypts gathered data and sends it to hxxp://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck, while a separate loader can retrieve a destination from a GitHub file and download and execute Python code without signature or hash verification. Container provenance for the affected build recorded the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm, rather than the legitimate BerriAI/litellm, and floating tags including latest, main-latest, and main-stable resolved to the affected image index at the time observed.

    The article advises organizations to block LiteLLM 1.107.0, stop deploying affected container tags or digests, and investigate systems where Python ran after installation. It recommends isolating affected hosts or containers, preserving useful evidence, rebuilding from reviewed artifacts, and replacing credentials that the process could have read. It also notes that removing the LiteLLM package alone may not remove top-level startup files or stop an already-running loader.

    • The malicious files were installed outside the main LiteLLM package directory, so simply removing the LiteLLM directory may leave Python startup hooks and an already-running background loader behind.
    • Starting Python or pip in an affected environment to investigate or remove the package can trigger the malware again; inspecting the wheel archive as data does not execute the startup hooks.
    • The release provenance recorded a nearly identical but different source repository, Berri-AI/litellm rather than BerriAI/litellm, and the malicious packaging configuration was absent from the tagged release, meaning a tag-only review could miss the change.
    • Floating container tags including latest, main-latest, and main-stable pointed to the affected image, so users could receive the compromised release without deliberately choosing version 1.107.0.
    • An empty remote-loader pointer prevents that component from downloading code at that moment, but it does not stop the separate credential collector or prevent a later pointer update from providing a download destination.
    Key Points
    • 01LiteLLM version 1.107.0 distributed malicious Python startup files in all seven published PyPI wheels, allowing the payload to run during normal Python startup without importing LiteLLM.
    • 02The payload collects cloud credentials, private keys, browser data, AI development-tool authentication files, environment variables, and LiteLLM proxy database records where accessible.
    • 03The collector sends encrypted archives to hxxp://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck and includes the fixed HTTP header X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb.
    • 04A separate sitecustomize.py component can retrieve a domain from a GitHub repository and download and execute Python code without signature or hash verification.
    • 05Published LiteLLM container tags including v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable resolved to the same affected image index at the time of observation.

    LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was compromised in Python wheels published on PyPI, and the official litellm/litellm:1.107.0 Docker image was also affected. The package contained an information-stealing program and a remote-control component that could execute attacker-provided code on infected systems. The article says users who installed the package version or ran the affected image, including through latest, main-latest, or main-stable tags, should assume their credentials were compromised.

    The malicious files were injected during the build process through a maturin configuration that included a cook/ directory not present in the source repository or source archive. The information stealer collected browser passwords, SSH keys, cloud credentials, environment variables, LiteLLM database data, and other secrets, while the background component checked hourly for commands to run.     • The infostealer’s one-time marker file can indicate that data collection already occurred, while the separate lock file can indicate that the command-fetching background process ran or remains active.
    • Users could receive the compromised Docker image through floating tags such as latest, main-latest, and main-stable, rather than explicitly selecting version 1.107.0.
    • The malicious collector targeted both locally stored credentials and credentials available from cloud-instance metadata services, expanding exposure beyond files saved on the machine.

    • 02The malicious files were inserted during the wheel build through a maturin configuration that bundled a directory absent from the source repository and source archive.

    • 04A separate startup file launched a background process that checked for attacker instructions every hour and could run arbitrary Python code with the privileges of the affected Python process.

In plain words

A harmful version of the popular LiteLLM software, version 1.107.0, was briefly published through PyPI and included in related container images. Anyone who installed or ran it could have had passwords, cloud access keys, developer tokens, browser data, and LiteLLM service keys copied from their computer or server. The hidden code also allowed the attacker to download and run more commands later, meaning the damage could go beyond stolen information. Because LiteLLM is widely used, affected people and organizations need to replace the software with a safe version and change any secrets the infected machine could access.

Summary
LiteLLM version 1.107.0 on PyPI and associated container images were compromised with startup hooks that stole credentials and could fetch and execute remote Python code. Organizations that installed or ran the affected release should remove the payload without starting Python, rebuild from a known-good pinned version, and rotate all accessible credentials.

On October 21, 2026, a malicious litellm version 1.107.0 was published to PyPI, and related Docker images also carried the payload. PyPI stopped serving the release in under two hours, while maintainers removed the malicious images by 14:32 UTC. The affected version was significant because LiteLLM had more than 92 million downloads in the preceding month and is used to call LLM provider APIs.

All seven compiled wheels installed cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py into the top level of Python’s site-packages, causing the payload to run whenever Python started, including when pip ran. The credential stealer collected browser data, cloud credentials, SSH keys, CI secrets, AI development tool tokens, process environment variables, and LiteLLM proxy credentials stored in a database when DATABASE_URL was configured. A separate loader could poll a GitHub-hosted file each hour, retrieve Python code from an attacker-controlled host, and execute it with the permissions of the process that launched Python.

The article advises affected users to remove the startup files before running Python again, stop the detached loader process, block the listed network infrastructure, and identify every host, virtual environment, cache, or container image that used the release. It recommends treating credentials accessible to an affected host as exposed, rotating them, reviewing cloud activity, and rebuilding environments from a pinned clean release such as litellm==1.106.2. It also notes that mutable image tags including latest, main-latest, and main-stable pointed to the malicious images before their removal.

  • The malicious files ran whenever Python started, even if LiteLLM was never imported, and this included running pip inside an affected environment.
  • Reinstalling a clean package from an infected Python environment could trigger the malicious startup hooks again, so the startup files needed to be removed before running Python.
  • The PyPI source distribution contained the altered build configuration but not the payload files, while every compiled wheel included them, making wheel inspection especially important.
  • A missing /tmp once-marker does not show that a host was unaffected because the marker was written only after a successful upload and temporary storage can disappear when a container restarts.
  • The malicious container payload was also reachable through mutable tags such as latest, main-latest, and main-stable, not only the explicit v1.107.0 tag.
Key Points
  • 01A malicious LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was uploaded to PyPI on October 21, 2026, and PyPI quarantined it in under two hours.
  • 02All seven malicious wheels installed a .pth startup hook, cook.py credential stealer, and sitecustomize.py remote code loader into the root of Python’s site-packages directory.
  • 03The credential stealer targeted browser data, SSH keys, cloud and container credentials, CI secrets, AI development tool tokens, process environment variables, and LiteLLM proxy database credentials when DATABASE_URL was set.
  • 04The loader polled a GitHub-hosted file hourly for a domain and could download and execute Python code from that domain with the permissions of the process that started Python.
  • 05The affected v1.107.0 Docker images and tags including latest, main-latest, and main-stable were removed after the maintainers confirmed the incident.

    PHP Patches Critical RCE Vulnerabilities, Organizations Urged to Take Unpatched Sites Offline
    socket.dev · 21 Oct 2026 15:28 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGSapache-http-servercalifcert-eucloudflarecve-2026-109618cve-2026-109619mod-phpnsaopenaiphpphp-fpmphp2shellunited-statesuse-after-freewiz
    In plain words

    PHP released emergency updates for two serious flaws that could let an outsider take control of websites and servers without signing in, and attackers are already testing ways to use them. The risk affects internet-facing sites that use PHP, including many sites built with WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and MediaWiki. Organizations need to update the underlying PHP software—not just their website or its add-ons—or temporarily remove affected sites from public access. The stakes are high because PHP powers a large share of the web, and many sites run old versions that may be difficult to update.

    Summary
    PHP has released emergency patches for two critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that can enable unauthenticated remote code execution on web servers, with attacks already observed. Organizations should upgrade the PHP runtime to fixed releases immediately or isolate internet-facing applications until patching is complete.

    PHP issued emergency updates on October 21 for two critical vulnerabilities collectively called PHP2Shell: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both flaws are rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale and can allow attackers to execute code on web servers without logging in. Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The NSA advised organizations unable to patch to take affected internet-facing systems offline, while CERT-EU recommended isolating applications from public networks.

    The issues affect PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, with affected paths reaching back to PHP 5.4. The demonstrated Apache mod_php path can be triggered before application code runs, and researchers also confirmed a PHP-FPM code-execution path during application execution. Cloudflare said it had already observed attack traffic and warned that its web application firewall rules are only a temporary stopgap. Updating WordPress, plugins, or frameworks alone is insufficient: organizations must update the PHP runtime and restart relevant services and long-running workers.

    • The highest-risk demonstrated attack path can be triggered through Apache mod_php before any website application code runs, meaning a well-maintained application can still be exposed through its underlying PHP runtime.
    • Nearly 48.5% of PHP websites in the cited W3Techs survey run PHP branches that no longer receive routine upstream security updates, although some may receive fixes from Linux distributions or long-term-support vendors.
    • PHP-FPM blocks the demonstrated mod_php startup sequence by exiting a worker after certain failures, but researchers confirmed a separate PHP-FPM path to code execution during application execution.
    • PHP published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 despite those versions being out of regular support, while emphasizing that this does not restore ongoing support.
    • Cloudflare made initial protective web-filtering rules available even to free-plan customers, but described them as a temporary stopgap rather than a complete fix.
    Key Points
    • 01PHP released emergency updates on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two PHP2Shell flaws rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 that can allow unauthenticated code execution on web servers.
    • 02The fixed PHP releases are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and organizations unable to patch were advised by the NSA and CERT-EU to take affected applications offline or isolate them from public networks.
    • 03Cloudflare reported observing attack traffic, including modified payloads intended to evade its protections, before the public release of the patches.
    • 04The vulnerabilities affect installations serving web requests through PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, with affected code paths dating back to PHP 5.4.
    • 05Updating a website application, framework, or plugin alone does not fix PHP2Shell; administrators must update the PHP runtime and restart relevant services and long-running workers.

    Two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, have CVSS v4.0 scores of 9.2 and are reported to be exploited in the wild. The article states that every unpatched PHP version is affected, with mod_php deployments considered the highest risk. PHP released fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

    Organizations should update PHP, restart PHP processes, and rebuild affected container images. Systems running PHP 8.1 or older need to upgrade to a supported release or obtain a vendor backport, while operating-system package users should check vendor changelogs for the CVE IDs because fixes may be backported without a version-number change. If updates cannot happen immediately, the article recommends applying both temporary settings, disabling session upload progress and setting the memory limit to unlimited, while noting that these measures do not make an installation safe.

    Both flaws involve PHP’s handling of out-of-memory errors during request processing. One can corrupt internal request data that PHP later treats as valid, while the other can leave stale request state available for use by a later request on the same worker. Because the flaws can expose worker memory, the article advises checking for compromise indicators and considering rotation of passwords, API keys, and tokens on internet-facing PHP systems.

    • The two temporary mitigations must be applied together because each addresses a different flaw; applying only one does not provide sufficient protection.
    • The article warns that the most definitive public exposure check can crash a PHP worker and interrupt requests, so it should be run outside peak hours.
    • PHP’s security team rates systems using mod_php as the highest-risk deployments for these flaws.
    • Because the flaws can expose PHP worker memory, the article recommends considering rotation of passwords, API keys, and tokens on internet-facing PHP systems even after patching.
    • Operating-system vendors may backport fixes without changing the displayed PHP version, so administrators should verify the CVE IDs in vendor package changelogs rather than relying only on version numbers.

    Cloudflare has launched full transaction detection and response rules for its WAF, allowing it to correlate suspicious HTTP requests with origin responses and block responses that indicate a successful exploit or data exposure. The capability is generally available to all plans, with initial managed protections targeting php2shell.

    Cloudflare has made full transaction detections and response rules generally available for its web application firewall, including on Free plans. Full transaction detections evaluate an HTTP request together with the response returned by the origin to identify evidence that an attempted exploit succeeded. Response rules can then block the origin response before it reaches the requester, replacing it with a WAF block page or custom response.

    The capability helps distinguish suspicious probing from cases in which an application exposes sensitive information, such as a path traversal request followed by a response containing a private database configuration file. Cloudflare says this can reduce the trade-off between broad request-only protections that may block legitimate traffic and narrower rules that can miss ambiguous activity. Its first managed transaction detections target the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability, and customers can investigate matching events in Security Events or create up to three custom response rules using Log or Block actions.

    • Correlating a suspicious request with the resulting response can distinguish an attempted exploit from evidence that sensitive information was actually exposed, reducing reliance on broad request-only signatures that may block legitimate traffic.
    • Blocking an origin response can prevent sensitive data from reaching the requester, but it cannot reverse actions that the origin application already performed.
    • Customers can review detection results in Security Analytics before creating enforcement policies, allowing them to scope rules to relevant paths, hosts, headers, or other application-specific conditions.
    • Response rules can be written to block only a successfully returned administration page, while allowing ordinary authentication failures, redirects, and unrelated traffic to proceed.
    • Although response rules are available on all plans, the response attack-detection fields used for more tailored custom policies are available to paying customers.
    Key Points

PHP disclosed two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to as php2shell, on 21 October 2026. Both received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 from the PHP project and affect every currently supported PHP branch before fixed releases. Because PHP underpins a large share of public websites and commonly supports WordPress, Magento, Drupal, and bespoke applications, the potential exposure is broad. Cloudflare reported observing attack traffic against customers, while public repositories have published code claiming to implement a working exploit.

CVE-2026-109618 stems from memory corruption after an out-of-memory condition, including conditions reachable through specially formed multipart requests. CVE-2026-109619 involves stale global state in persistent PHP workers after failures such as parse errors, failed requires, timeouts, or out-of-memory events, with confirmed paths involving fatal error backtraces and session upload progress handling. PHP released fixes in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12, and states that updating is the only complete mitigation. Organizations should prioritize Apache mod_php deployments, assess relevant PHP-FPM configurations, rebuild container images, confirm managed WAF rules are blocking, and treat end-of-life PHP installations as urgent migration cases.

  • External scans can identify where PHP is reachable but generally cannot determine the server mode or configuration settings that govern exploitability, so organizations need configuration-management data to prioritize risk accurately.
  • Older, unsupported PHP installations should be treated as urgent even though they fall outside the PHP project’s listed supported-version ranges, because they may be affected without receiving a fix and already contain years of unpatched issues.
  • A system can be patched even if it still reports an older upstream PHP version because operating-system vendors may backport fixes, while rebuilt containers can remain vulnerable if they use stale image layers.
  • Cloudflare’s WAF protections provide useful temporary coverage, but attackers were already modifying their request payloads to evade detection, making software updates necessary rather than optional.

In plain words

The Lazarus Group, a suspected North Korean-linked hacking group, used convincing fake job résumé and design websites to target at least three South Korean companies in software, construction, and communications equipment. Visiting the sites may have abused a commonly required South Korean banking and government security program, allowing the attackers to secretly install tools that can gather information, steal browser data, and control infected computers. This matters because the campaign shows how widely installed security software can become a gateway for espionage, and the attackers are rapidly improving and reusing their tools across multiple campaigns.

Summary
Kaspersky reports that Lazarus Group’s Operation FlashHole targeted South Korean organizations by abusing mandatory CrossWeb EX security software and tailored phishing sites to deliver a highly modular, largely memory-resident malware chain. The campaign combines updated TechHub, Cubridge, TouchShift, ClientHub, and LPEClient tooling with GitHub- and compromised-site-based C2 infrastructure for espionage and payload delivery.

Kaspersky describes Operation FlashHole, a Lazarus Group campaign that targeted at least three South Korean organizations in the software, construction, and wired communication equipment sectors. The earliest evidence dates to July 2025, and the campaign followed Operation SyncHole while expanding into different industries. Researchers assess with medium-to-high confidence that targets received spear-phishing emails linking to tailored GitHub Pages sites posing as a job seeker’s résumé or an interior design portfolio. The sites contained external malicious JavaScript and may have initiated infection involving the mandatory financial-security product CrossWeb EX.

The infection chain executed fsquirt.exe under the CrossWeb EX service process and injected shellcode containing TechHub, with much of the initial chain existing only in memory. TechHub used private GitHub repositories for command-and-control communication, while later payloads included Cubridge, TouchHub, TouchShift, ClientHub, and LPEClient. Persistence involved DLL side-loading through a malicious mscoree.dll and a service created from a legitimate Windows executable, allowing TouchShift to run with SYSTEM privileges. Cubridge and ClientHub could load tools and plugins for activities including process and browser-data collection, Active Directory queries, file collection and archiving, file deletion, and remote-session monitoring.

The article highlights LPEClient as a longstanding Lazarus tool that was substantially updated to profile systems, inspect patch and security-mitigation status, and receive payloads through ClientHub. Its communication used several cryptographic methods, including ML-KEM-1024 post-quantum key encapsulation, GOST, and Threefish, before reflectively loading Cubridge in memory. Kaspersky links FlashHole to the broader Cascade Hole campaign and to Lazarus’s Dream Job-related toolsets, while distinguishing it from concurrent COPPERHEDGE activity associated with ransomware and data exfiltration. The researchers expect attacks abusing South Korea’s mandatory security software to remain active until that software is eliminated or mitigated.

  • The attackers used private GitHub repositories as a command-and-control channel, with TechHub creating and updating GitHub issues and exchanging encrypted files through repository filenames and content.
  • Much of the initial infection chain operated only in memory, while the few persistent files were disguised through DLL side-loading and legitimate Windows binaries running as services with SYSTEM privileges.
  • LPEClient’s updated version checks Windows patch-level information and low-level security protections, including Kernel VA Shadow and Shadow Stack status, before receiving later-stage payloads.
  • The campaign used several cryptographic methods, including ML-KEM-1024 post-quantum key encapsulation, to protect payload delivery; Kaspersky noted that this adoption outpaced many legitimate security products.
  • South Korea’s plan to phase out mandatory security-software installation beginning in 2026 may leave the currently installed software an attractive attack route until it is eliminated or mitigated.

In plain words

Eight digital certificates from eMudhra, a company that helps prove websites and software are genuine, were found to have easily guessed secret keys. Someone with those keys could create fake certificates to pose as real websites or sign software, potentially letting them intercept or alter information. Major browser makers and Microsoft have blocked the affected certificates, but other software, VPNs, devices, and services may still trust them unless they receive updates. The issue shows why organizations need to update their software and certificate lists as fixes become available.

Summary
Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were compromised by critically weak P-384 key generation, allowing attackers to forge trusted TLS or code-signing certificates. Organizations should apply vendor updates—particularly Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10—and verify that affected certificate chains are blocked across non-browser systems.

Cisco Talos reported that eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority certificates were compromised because their private keys were generated with critically weak randomness. The flaw occurred during an April 30, 2025 key-generation activity under the emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and cross-signed Comodo AAA Certificate Services. During a wrap/unwrap step for 24 subordinate CAs, a second set of weak P-384 keys was created and mistakenly used for eight intermediates. eMudhra revoked the affected certificates and stopped issuing certificates under its G3 root.

Six of the affected certificates were used for TLS and have been blocked by Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple, while two code-signing certificates have also been blocked by Microsoft. An attacker with one of the compromised intermediate private keys could issue fraudulent certificates to impersonate websites or services, potentially intercepting or modifying traffic where affected keys remain trusted. Go designated the issue CVE-2026-111943 and released Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10, which reject certificate chains containing the compromised intermediate keys. Talos recommends updating software and trust stores, particularly for applications, VPNs, embedded devices, and cloud-native environments that may use separate certificate stores or ignore revocation information.

  • Browser-level blocking does not necessarily protect applications that use separate, stale, embedded, or legacy certificate stores and do not check revocations.
  • The Go fixes explicitly reject certificate chains containing the compromised intermediate keys, addressing cloud-native and static-container environments where normal certificate revocation may be ignored.
  • A forged TLS certificate could enable package-registry impersonation, but it would not by itself defeat separate package-integrity controls such as lockfile hashes, checksums, signatures, or provenance verification.
  • Embedded and industrial devices may require vendor updates or other compensating measures because their certificate stores and update mechanisms can be independently managed or limited.
Key Points
  • 01Eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised after a flawed April 30, 2025 key-generation process produced weak P-384 private keys with only 3 to 8 bits of entropy.
  • 02Six affected TLS intermediate certificates have been blocked by Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple, while two affected Microsoft code-signing certificates have also been blocked.
  • 03eMudhra revoked the compromised certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its emSign Root TLS CA - G3 root.
  • 04The Go project released Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10 for CVE-2026-111943, filtering certificate chains containing the eight compromised eMudhra intermediate keys.
  • 05Cisco Talos had not observed malicious use of the compromised certificates in the wild as of October 21, 2026.

This is a high-impact certificate authority incident involving eight compromised intermediate certificates that could enable trusted TLS or code-signing impersonation. Although no malicious use had been observed, the exposure affects browsers, Go-based cloud-native environments, VPNs, appliances, and systems with independently managed trust stores.

Summary
Drupal released fixes for CVE-2026-108097, a critical Field UI remote code execution flaw that becomes exploitable when contributed or custom code passes request-influenced data into vulnerable render rows. Update to the fixed core release for your branch immediately, or uninstall Field UI as a temporary workaround while auditing custom and contributed modules.

Drupal disclosed CVE-2026-108097, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the core Field UI module, in security advisory SA-CORE-2026-014 on 14 October 2026. The flaw occurs because a callback associated with a Field UI table row could be executed as PHP code rather than treated as a declared value. Drupal says core by itself is not directly exploitable, but contributed or custom code can create an exploit path if it allows request-influenced data to reach the affected render-array key.

The issue affects broad Drupal core ranges across supported 10.x and 11.x branches, as well as specified Drupal 12 pre-releases. Drupal released fixes in versions 10.6.19, 11.3.19, and 11.4.10, while Drupal 12 pre-release users should move to 12.0.0-beta2 or later. Organizations that cannot immediately upgrade can uninstall Field UI as a workaround, and should inventory internet-facing sites, include staging and test systems, and review contributed and custom modules for the affected data flow.

  • Although Drupal rates the issue as critical, its exploit maturity is theoretical, and independent researchers reported finding no public contributed module using the vulnerable pattern after demonstrating it with a lab-built bridge module.
  • A site’s Drupal version determines whether it needs the patch, but not whether it is directly exploitable; that depends on whether custom or contributed code passes request-influenced data into the affected Field UI table row.
  • Uninstalling Field UI can provide a practical temporary safeguard because the module is used to manage content types and display settings rather than to serve normal site pages.
  • Staging, test, and demo sites merit the same priority as production because they commonly share production code and modules while falling outside normal release schedules.

The Gentlemen is a Russian-speaking ransomware-as-a-service group that emerged in mid-2025 after reportedly operating as an affiliate of LockBit and Qilin. A vendor bank-change BEC email used a newly registered lookalike domain while embedding legitimate vendor links, so URL scans and hover checks appeared safe. The fraud was exposed by inconsistent, recently edited PDF metadata and conflicting bank and contact details, underscoring the need for out-of-band verification of payment changes.

A diversified holding company received a vendor bank-change request from mackyacomm.com, a lookalike domain registered 28 days earlier. The message asked recipients to use a new bank account for future payments and included two PDF attachments. Its links appeared legitimate: the website URLs led to the real vendor and the signature email link opened a message to a real vendor employee. As a result, link scanners found no malicious destination.

The fraud indicators were in the sender identity and documents rather than the links. A Chase letter printed with a 2026 date had a 2025 source creation date and was modified on the morning of the send, while the second PDF was a 2019 office scan edited that same morning. The PDFs also conflicted on the bank branch, the signer’s job title, and phone details. A human analyst marked the emails malicious and removed all four copies, although a later automated review labeled the message safe based on the clean links.

  • A clean hover result can be misleading when the visible sender information is altered but the underlying links still point to a legitimate vendor site.
  • Email authentication passing for a lookalike domain only shows that the sender was authorized to use that false domain; it does not establish that the sender represents the genuine vendor.
  • Document metadata can provide useful verification evidence when a printed date, original creation date, and same-day modification history do not align.
  • For bank-detail changes, independently calling a vendor contact already on file is more reliable than trusting links, signatures, or attachments included in the request.
  • The article shows that automated analysis focused on clean links may reach a different conclusion than human review that considers sender identity and document inconsistencies.

vlt 1.5.0 introduces vlt skills, a command for discovering agent skill folders in already installed JavaScript dependencies and linking selected skills into project directories read by coding agents. Skills contain a SKILL.md file with instructions for working with a tool or library, but would otherwise remain inside node_modules. By default, vlt targets .agents/skills and can also link into detected agent-specific directories such as .claude/skills.

Developers can list a package’s available skills, approve selected packages or individual skills with the :skill() selector, and save those choices as allow-skills in vlt.json. vlt maintains the links as dependencies change, using the installed package version recorded in the project lockfile, and vlt ci applies the saved configuration for cloned repositories. Linking is opt-in, and when no selection is saved, vlt skills link excludes packages marked by Socket’s high-confidence malware alerts; teams can also filter out packages flagged for typosquatting, vulnerabilities, or obfuscated code.

  • The :skill() selector allows teams to approve individual instruction sets within a package rather than accepting every skill the package provides.

It recommends practical safeguards such as waiting before accepting brand-new updates, locking software to known versions, limiting who can publish updates, and protecting developers’ computers. Summary
To reduce software supply chain risk, enforce package cooldowns and install-script controls, pin dependencies and CI/container references, and tightly scope access, developer endpoints, and AI agents. Back these controls with install-time and repository scanning, signed SBOMs, audit logs, and rehearsed credential-rotation procedures.

In the second quarter of 2026, Aikido Intel analyzed about 7.5 million package versions and confirmed 19,500 malicious packages. The article says supply chain attacks surged in mid-2025, with compromises involving widely used packages and tools including axios, Trivy, and Checkmarx. It presents controls intended to stop the attacks seen over the previous 18 months, beginning with a 48-hour minimum package age and blocking dependency install scripts. A cooldown can prevent adoption of newly published malicious releases while detection systems have time to flag and remove them.

The guide recommends committing and enforcing lockfiles, pinning CI dependencies to commit SHAs, and pinning container base images to immutable digests so upstream references cannot silently change. It also calls for narrowly scoped tokens, separate pipeline credentials, FIDO2 or passkeys for maintainers, endpoint protection on developer machines, and centrally managed allowlists for IDE and browser extensions. For AI agents, it recommends limiting permissions, isolating runtime environments, treating MCP servers as dependencies, and treating untrusted text reaching an agent as if it could trigger harmful actions. Finally, organizations should stream audit logs, generate signed software bills of materials for each build, and rehearse credential-rotation procedures so they can identify exposure and respond quickly when a malicious package is discovered.

  • A 48-hour package delay would have prevented adoption of the malicious Axios releases while leaving roughly 45 hours before npm removed them, but the article notes that at least one CanisterWorm package went undetected for about 53 hours, so the delay should be paired with install-time detection.
  • Pinning is not a one-time solution: commit-SHA and container-digest pins stop silent upstream changes, but teams must deliberately update them on a schedule to receive upstream fixes.
  • Developer computers are a critical supply-chain target because they commonly hold source code, cloud credentials, publishing tokens, and active sessions to infrastructure.
  • An approved extension list can block unknown fake extensions, but it cannot protect against a legitimate approved extension that later becomes compromised and updates automatically.
  • AI coding agents can be tricked into installing attacker-registered package names that the agent invented, so checks are needed both when software is installed and before a new dependency is merged into a repository.
Key Points
  • 01Apply a 48-hour minimum age for newly published package versions, because many compromised releases are detected and removed within hours of publication.
  • 02Disable dependency installation scripts where possible, since package postinstall hooks can execute code with the installer’s privileges.
  • 03Use committed lockfiles, commit-SHA pins for CI dependencies, and digest pins for container base images to prevent unapproved upstream changes from being pulled automatically.
  • 04Protect maintainer and developer accounts with narrowly scoped credentials, separate pipeline tokens, and FIDO2 security keys or passkeys.
  • 05Prepare for malicious-package incidents by streaming audit logs, creating signed software component inventories for build artifacts, and rehearsing credential-rotation procedures.

Because these were application identities rather than user accounts, the activity did not produce familiar signs such as suspicious MFA prompts or interactive user logins. The incident illustrates how a compromised third-party integration can give an attacker access through an identity the tenant already trusts.

The article recommends hunting beyond known IP addresses and application IDs by looking for unusual application sign-ins, changes in source infrastructure, dormant applications becoming active, and unexpected token requests. It emphasizes correlating suspicious authentication with privileged directory changes, such as role assignments or permission expansion, and with new secrets or certificates added to other applications. This correlation is important because credentials added to secondary applications can preserve access even after the original compromised integration is disabled or its credentials are rotated.

  • A successful service-principal sign-in proves that an application authenticated, but it does not by itself prove that the activity was authorized because the logs may not reveal who operated the application credentials.
  • Activity that appears routine in one tenant can become a strong incident signal when the same application signs in from new infrastructure across many tenants.
  • Microsoft Graph read activity is not always recorded as an Entra audit event, so the absence of logged resource access does not prove that no directory data was read.
  • Rotating or disabling the originally compromised application may not remove access if an attacker previously added independent credentials to other application identities.
  • The strongest detection sequence links an unusual application sign-in to a privileged directory change, credential creation on another application, and later authentication through that secondary identity.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers used stolen ConnectWise application credentials on October 15, 2026, to sign into customers’ Microsoft 365 tenants as ConnectWise applications, with unauthorized sign-ins confirmed in at least 162 tenants.
  • 02Application identities can authenticate with credentials, certificates, or federated identities and access resources without an interactive user sign-in, so user-focused indicators such as MFA prompts may not appear.
  • 03A suspicious application sign-in should be correlated with administrative actions such as privileged role assignments and the creation of credentials on other applications.
  • 04An attacker who adds a client secret or certificate to another application can retain access through that secondary application after the original compromised integration is disabled.
  • 05Effective containment requires checking for residual credentials, unreversed privileged role assignments, active OAuth grants, and continued authentication through secondary applications.

In plain words

Tenable changed its AI security service so it can recognize dangerous or policy-breaking requests in 10 languages without first translating every request into English. It created carefully checked translated examples to train one model that can spot threats such as attempts to bypass AI safeguards, harmful content, and attempts to obtain sensitive data. This matters to organizations using AI in multiple countries, because attackers can write harmful requests in many languages and translation can be slow, costly, or change the meaning of a request.

Summary
Tenable replaced its translate-then-detect workflow with a single multilingual security detection model trained using an agentic, label-preserving translation pipeline. The company says the approach supports 10 validated languages while reducing latency and operating costs substantially without sacrificing detection quality.

Tenable describes how it added native multilingual support to the security detectors in Tenable One AI Exposure. Its earlier process identified a language, translated non-English input into English with a large translation model, and then applied an English detector. Tenable says that approach added latency, cost, operational overhead, and risked losing security-relevant meaning during translation.

To train a single multilingual model, Tenable built an agentic translation pipeline that creates label-preserving translations of English training and benchmark data into nine additional languages. A frontier model produces context-aware translations, independent judges assess fluency, meaning integrity, and whether the label remains valid, and failed items are refined; sensitive items refused by the frontier model are sent to a controlled open-source small-language model and evaluated through the same gate. Tenable fine-tuned a compact model already pretrained on many languages and says its resulting detector supports 10 validated languages, runs in tens of milliseconds, and matched or exceeded the prior translate-then-detect approach on the reported threat-detection benchmarks.

  • Translation quality must preserve the original security label, because a translation can soften malicious intent or otherwise change a dangerous example into one that appears harmless, creating mislabeled training data.
  • Tenable tested whether its pretrained multilingual model could generalize from English before paying to create translated data; for some tasks it did, and training on only a handful of languages also improved performance in other languages.
  • The pipeline uses a controlled open-source small language model when a frontier model refuses sensitive content, so security-relevant examples involving topics such as weapons synthesis or self-harm are not silently excluded from the dataset.
  • Tenable reports that producing multilingual training and benchmark data cost under $10,000 once, unlike an always-on translation service whose cost increases with every customer request.
  • Although Tenable says its model can read and flag inputs in thousands of languages beyond those used in training, it has formally validated only 10 languages and says the wider capability needs further testing before it can be relied on.
Key Points
  • 01Tenable One AI Exposure previously translated non-English inputs into English before running its security detectors, which added latency, cost, operational overhead, and potential loss of security-relevant meaning.
  • 02Tenable built an agentic translation pipeline that transcreates labeled English data into target languages, uses independent judges to assess fluency, meaning preservation, and label integrity, and refines or reroutes failed and refused translations.
  • 03The company fine-tuned a compact model pretrained on many languages, translating training data only for languages and tasks where English-only training did not generalize sufficiently.
  • 04Tenable states that its single multilingual model natively supports English plus Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, and Hindi, with detection running in tens of milliseconds.
  • 05According to Tenable, the multilingual model matched or exceeded translate-then-detect AI-threat detection on 9 of 10 languages and led on every language for harmful-content detection at the reported false-positive rates.

It notes that unmanaged assets, IoT devices, and OT equipment often cannot run security agents or be easily patched, making the network an important control layer. code change concept

patching concept

personal information concept

pinned concept

plugin concept

Portuguese is a language spoken mainly in Portugal, Brazil, and several other countries.

private data concept
Sensitive information that should not be publicly disclosed, like personal identifiers or financial records.

Private information is personal or confidential data that should not be shared without permission.
private key concept

privileges concept
Privileges are permissions that determine what actions a user or process is allowed to perform on a system.

project files concept
Project files are documents, code, settings, or other files related to a specific piece of work.

prompts concept

public services concept

ransom concept

Remote Code Execution Vulnerabilities concept
Flaws that can let an attacker run their own commands or programs on another system.

Remote-code-execution flaws are vulnerabilities that can let an attacker run commands on a system from afar.

repository concept

resilience concept
The ability of an organization to anticipate, withstand, and recover from adverse cyber events and security breaches.

scans concept
